title: The Lasser Glass
summary: The haunted mirror from Oculus has turned up, or been reported, in nearly every Flanagan work since, and Flanagan has confirmed many of the sightings himself.
description:
The Lasser Glass began as a plastic mirror bought online for Flanagan's 2006 short and became the antagonist of Oculus, rebuilt by designer Bruce Larsen with a frame Flanagan describes as "writhing humanoid forms." He pitched the feature as a "portable Overlook Hotel," and he keeps hiding the mirror in later work to keep its mythology alive for a follow-up that has been stuck since Relativity Media's bankruptcy left the rights murky. Sources disagree on how many physical mirrors exist (one report says two were built, one living at Flanagan's home and one that travels to sets; another says one broke), so treat the count as unsettled.

Not every sighting is equal. Ouija: Origin of Evil, Gerald's Game, Doctor Sleep, Midnight Mass and The Midnight Club are confirmed by Flanagan on the record; Hill House, Bly Manor and the Usher bar appearance are reported by several outlets; the Absentia sighting rests on a single review. Flanagan has said it is not in The Life of Chuck, and no one has reported it in Hush, Before I Wake, or Carrie (a frame-by-frame check of Carrie is still open). The carved dining chairs in Usher resemble the frame but are a different design. One correction to common copy: the Usher chest tattoo is on Rahul Kohli's Leo Usher, not on Owen, his Bly Manor character.

The headboard Jessie is cuffed to is built from the bottom edge of the mirror's frame, mounted upside down per one report. Confirmed by Flanagan to Den of Geek and on Twitter, and by Trevor Macy to Rue Morgue.

Half under a sheet on the rec center stage behind the AA meetings; around 9:00 is a clear view (per ComicBook.com). Confirmed by Flanagan to Entertainment Weekly: "It's behind them in the profile [shots] on stage."

title: Maddie Young's novel Midnight Mass
summary: Years before the series existed, a horror novel called Midnight Mass by Hush's heroine sits on shelves in Hush and Gerald's Game.
description:
In Hush, a friend returns Maddie Young's (Kate Siegel) hardback of her own novel and we see the back cover: "the 512 souls on sleepy Crocket[t]" island and a church that brings "Riley face to face with a terrifying secret." The cover also carries a fake blurb credited to producer Trevor Macy. In Gerald's Game the same cover sits on the shelf above the bed, and Jessie grabs it to throw at the stray dog.

Flanagan spent more than a decade developing Midnight Mass as a novel and then a script before Netflix made it in 2021, so the prop is a promise he kept. CBR and Capital both point out a consequence: because Midnight Mass is a book inside Hush and Gerald's Game, the series cannot share their universe.

title: One mould, two monsters
summary: The smiling white mask in Hush was cast from the mould Bruce Larsen made for the Canker Man's face in Before I Wake.
description:
Flanagan explained it on his Tumblr: "The HUSH mask was designed by Bruce Larsen, who also designed the OCULUS mirror, and the Canker Man character from BEFORE I WAKE. The mask in HUSH is actually based on the Canker Man's face from that movie. We used the mold for the creature design that Bruce had made." The mask was softened to look more human, and he added that it was not modelled on Kate Siegel's face.

Larsen also built the Gerald's Game headboard from the Lasser Glass frame, which makes him the person behind most of Flanagan's recurring objects.

title: Hill House's hidden ghosts
summary: Ghosts stand in the background of almost every Hill House episode, unremarked and often out of focus, and Flanagan says they were part of the pitch from the start.
description:
Flanagan says hiding ghosts in plain sight was in the original pitch, with "dozens" per episode, and ghost extras were on set every day. The design team also "tried to use design elements that look like human faces everywhere we could," in the wallpaper, light fixtures and doorknobs. Writer Jeff Howard says the team knows why each ghost is where it is, even though the show never explains them.

Counts disagree: NME lists 33, IMDb Originals 43, Looper "over three dozen." The per-episode list here follows NME, cross-listed by BuzzFeed, Higgypop and others; individual sightings are widely reported, not confirmed shot by shot, and timestamps vary between encodes. NME lists none for episodes 6 and 8.

title: The Bent-Neck Lady
summary: The ghost that terrorised Nell all her life turns out to be Nell herself, falling back through time after her death in Hill House.
description:
From childhood, Nell is visited by a woman with a broken, twisted neck. In "The Bent-Neck Lady" the show reveals that it is her own ghost: when she hangs herself in the Red Room, her neck snaps and she falls back through her own life, landing in the moments when her younger self woke paralysed in fear. It turns every earlier sighting into a scene of Nell watching herself.

The episode is full of Shirley Jackson as well. Nerdist reads the staircase deaths and Nell's dance as a nod to Eleanor on the novel's spiral stair, and Cheatsheet places the Lasser Glass in the room during the dance (reported, not confirmed). NME also counts three hidden ghosts in the episode.

title: Usher's Poe names
summary: Nearly every name in Usher comes from Poe's stories, poems or life, from Verna (an anagram of raven) to Arthur Pym.
description:
Verna is an anagram of "raven." Tamerlane is a Poe poem; Victorine LaFourcade comes from "The Premature Burial"; Camille L'Espanaye from "Rue Morgue"; Napoleon "Leo" from "The Spectacles"; Prospero "Perry" from "Masque"; Bill-T Wilson from "William Wilson"; Morella and Lenore from the stories and poems of those names; Annabel Lee from the poem Roderick recites as if he wrote it. C. Auguste Dupin is Poe's detective, here standing in for the story's narrator; Arthur Pym is from Poe's only novel; Alessandra Ruiz from Politian; Toby from "Never Bet the Devil Your Head" ("Damn it, Toby!"); Fortunato Pharmaceuticals from "The Cask of Amontillado." Frederick's source is disputed: Den of Geek says "Metzengerstein," Wikipedia ties the rivalry to Rufus Griswold instead. Creepy Catalog's reading of the drug Ligadone as "Ligeia" is fan theory.

Real people show up too: Eliza (Poe's mother), Rufus Griswold (Poe's actual rival, here walled up like Fortunato), William Longfellow and Judge John Neal.

title: Books on the shelves
summary: Flanagan's sets are stocked with telling books: Pike and King in Midnight Mass, The Gunslinger in The Midnight Club, Jackson in Hill House, The Exorcist in Carrie.
description:
Books are the cheapest way to plant a reference, and Flanagan's set dressers use them often. The best documented are Ed Flynn reading Stephen King's Revival in Midnight Mass, a novel about a preacher's costly miracles that Flanagan was once attached to adapt (reported by Screen Rant and BuzzFeed), and Kevin pulling The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger from his locker in The Midnight Club (on Netflix's own list of the show's eggs).

The others rest on a single outlet each. Riley's childhood shelf holds a Christopher Pike book, a year before Flanagan adapted Pike, and King paperbacks including 'Salem's Lot, beside Se7en and Dana Scully posters. Leeza reads Always and Forever, Lara Jean, from the Netflix franchise whose sequels were directed by Flanagan's cinematographer Michael Fimognari. Nell reads a Shirley Jackson book. And in Carrie a student has The Exorcist open in the library, as Flanagan's own Exorcist film was in the works.
